content.overview: Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 declares a marriage null and void if it contravenes s. 5(i) (living spouse), s. 5(iv) (prohibited degrees) or s. 5(v) (sapinda relationship), unless custom governing both parties permits the latter two. The marriage is void ab initio; a decree of nullity is commonly sought for status and consequential reliefs. Children receive limited legitimacy under s. 16.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Living spouse? (2) Prohibited degrees / custom? (3) Sapinda / custom? (4) Decree of nullity for status? (5) s. 16 children? (6) vs voidable s. 12?
content.study:
Section 11 provides that any marriage solemnised after the commencement of the Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition by either party against the other, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes s. 5(i), (iv) or (v).

Grounds: living spouse (bigamy); prohibited degrees without saving custom; sapinda without saving custom.

Void ab initio — no marital status arises. Parties ordinarily obtain a formal decree for clarity, records, and consequential reliefs (ss. 24–25). Children receive limited legitimacy under s. 16. Bigamy also attracts s. 17 criminal liability.

Custom may save only prohibited degrees and sapinda, not bigamy.

No case authority invented. Case-law verification remains a separate gate.

sections.heading: Three grounds of voidness
sections.body: s. 5(i) living spouse; s. 5(iv) prohibited degrees; s. 5(v) sapinda. Custom may save only the last two.

sections.heading: Void ab initio
sections.body: No marital status arises. The decree of nullity is declaratory of existing nullity, not constitutive of a new status.

sections.heading: Custom exception limits
sections.body: Custom cannot validate a bigamous marriage under s. 5(i). It applies only to (iv) and (v) and must govern both parties.

sections.heading: Children and consequential reliefs
sections.body: s. 16 confers limited legitimacy. Maintenance under ss. 24–25 may be claimed in appropriate cases.

sections.heading: Contrast with s. 12
sections.body: Voidable marriages under s. 12 are valid until annulled; void marriages under s. 11 never acquire marital status.

examples.title: Bigamy
examples.body: Second ceremony while first marriage subsists — void under s. 11 read with s. 5(i); s. 17 may also apply.

examples.title: Prohibited degrees without custom
examples.body: Marriage within prohibited degrees with no saving custom — void under s. 11 read with s. 5(iv).

hypotheticals.question: Does a void marriage require a court order?
hypotheticals.analysis: It is void ab initio, but parties ordinarily seek a formal decree of nullity for status, records, and consequential reliefs.

distinctions.title: Void (s. 11) vs Voidable (s. 12)
distinctions.left: Void ab initio; no marital status.

rows.right: Impotence, s. 5(ii), force/fraud, pregnancy by another (with bars)

misconceptions.trap: A void marriage needs no court order.
misconceptions.correction: A formal decree is still ordinarily obtained for status, records, and consequential reliefs.

misconceptions.trap: Custom can save a bigamous marriage.
misconceptions.correction: Custom saves only prohibited degrees and sapinda, not monogamy under s. 5(i).
